claim: Only a handful of icons (home, print, magnifying-glass search) have near-universal recognition; all other icons are ambiguous across interfaces, so every icon needs an accompanying text label — especially for novice/senior users who lack learned conventions.
verbatim_quote: There are a few icons that enjoy mostly universal recognition from users. The icons for home, print, and the magnifying glass for search are such instances. Outside of these examples, most icons continue to be ambiguous to users due to their association with different meanings across various interfaces.

claim: Icon text labels must be visible at all times without user interaction; hover-revealed labels do not work on touch devices, so GranPhone must use permanent labels under/beside icons.
verbatim_quote: Icon labels should be visible at all times, without any interaction from the user. For navigation icons, labels are particularly critical. Don't rely on hover to reveal text labels: not only does it increase the interaction cost, but it also fails to translate well on touch devices.

claim: For older adults specifically, text labels on icons and buttons help them memorize functions, locations, and navigation paths.
verbatim_quote: text labels for icons and buttons can also help older adults memorize functions, locations, and navigation paths
notes: Li & Luximon, BIT 2019, literature-review statement citing multiple prior studies.

claim: The hamburger icon fails with seniors: in a 22-participant older-adult study, 11 could not understand the hamburger icon and the side-drawer entry task saw 29% breakdowns plus 29% complete failures — metaphorical/abstract icons must be avoided or always labelled.
verbatim_quote: 11 participants could not understand the meaning of hamburger icon. 9 participants could not find the entry point of side drawer at first
notes: Numeric finding; also note participants were high-digital-literacy seniors, so novice users likely worse.

claim: Older adults navigate more effectively through visible content than through menus, icons, and buttons; content-oriented navigation design outperformed menu-oriented patterns in understanding, navigation, and interaction for seniors.
verbatim_quote: overall older adults were able to navigate using contents more effectively than menus and buttons... the content-oriented navigation design performed better in understanding, navigation, and interaction
notes: Supports big labelled content cards over icon toolbars in GranPhone.

claim: Removing clickability signifiers (flat/ghost styling) measurably hurts findability: eyetracking experiment (n=71) showed 22% longer time and 25% more fixations on weak-signifier pages vs strong-signifier ones.
verbatim_quote: On average participants spent 22% more time (i.e., slower task performance) looking at the pages with weak signifiers... On average, people had 25% more fixations on the pages with weak signifiers.
notes: General web users on desktop; senior effect plausibly larger but untested.

claim: Older adults struggle to distinguish touchable from non-touchable elements: study found seniors 'could not correctly distinguish between the touchable and non-touchable text' and generally have problems 'differentiating which areas could be touched and which could not.'
verbatim_quote: 3 users could not correctly distinguish between the touchable and non-touchable text
notes: Reinforces need for unambiguous persistent tappability signifiers.

claim: Elevation/shadow alone does NOT signal tappability to seniors: participants seldom noticed or tapped a floating action button despite its shadow cue, plausibly because declined visual perception impairs reading 3D depth cues; prior studies found older adults prefer raised buttons with visual highlighting and immediate feedback.
verbatim_quote: Participants reported that they seldom noticed or tapped this button though the floating action button provides an obvious visual cue through the use of shadows. The reason may lie at the decreased visual perception influenced older adults' ability to understand the depth cues of 3D shapes.
notes: Author's causal explanation is hedged in the paper itself; the behavioral finding (FAB unnoticed) is direct. Implication: use filled colored buttons + labels, not just elevation.

claim: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 requires icons and UI-component visuals needed to understand content/identify controls to have at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors — this is the hard floor for GranPhone icon strokes and button boundaries.
verbatim_quote: The visual presentation of the following have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent color(s): User Interface Components: Visual information required to identify user interface components and states... Graphical Objects: Parts of graphics required to understand the content
notes: Web standard, but standard practice applies it to native apps too.

claim: Thin-line icon strokes lose effective contrast through anti-aliasing on screen, so for low-vision users filled or thick-stroke pictograms are safer than thin outlined icons.
verbatim_quote: Due to anti-aliasing, particularly thin lines and shapes of non-text elements may be rendered with reduced contrast.
notes: Inference from the WCAG warning about thin lines; combined with 3:1 requirement, thin-outlined icon families are risky on cheap 2017-era screens.

claim: Color must never be the only signal: WCAG 1.4.1 forbids using color alone to indicate an action, and icons/symbols should differ by shape as well as color — accept/reject call buttons need distinct glyph shapes and positions in addition to green/red.
verbatim_quote: Icons and symbols should differ by shape as well as by color.

claim: The green=good/red=bad convention is strong but not colorblind-safe: red-green colorblind users cannot reliably distinguish pure red vs pure green; recommended fixes are adding a redundant non-color cue and/or shifting hues (reddish-orange vs bluish-green) while keeping the cultural semantics.
verbatim_quote: Users with red-green color blindness have trouble distinguishing red and green... Avoid pure red and green in this situation; a reddish-orange and a bluish-green are distinguishable by color blind users, while still conveying the cultural 'good' and 'bad' meanings to users with normal color vision.
notes: Directly applicable to accept/reject call buttons.

claim: Colorblind users still understand red/green symbolism and designers should retain meaningful colors rather than strip them: interviews with red-green-deficient users found 'color blind people still understand color symbolism'; recommendations — keep meaningful colors, be consistent, allow customization.
verbatim_quote: Interfaces should retain meaningful colors, consistency is critical, and customization is ideal.
notes: Honors thesis, n=4 interviews — directional only. Conclusion: keep green/red phone conventions AND redundant shape/label/position cues.

claim: Tappability guidance for flat/modern UIs: buttons should 'vaguely look like physical buttons', avoid ghost buttons (thin outline, no fill), never style interactive and static elements identically, reserve a consistent treatment for clickable items, and pair icons with label text.
verbatim_quote: Make sure your buttons at least vaguely look like physical buttons. Avoid ghost buttons — text with a thin rectangular outline... With few exceptions, these icons should be paired with label text.
notes: Maps to Material filled/tonal buttons rather than outlined/text buttons for seniors.

claim: Voice input is NOT effortless for seniors: in a study of 18 adults 74+, most follow-up reactions were unfavorable — participants kept forgetting the wake word and 'struggled to compose a concise command sentence,' speaking long unstructured sentences that the assistant failed on.
verbatim_quote: many participants kept forgetting to start a command with a wake word or confused the wake word with other similar words... many participants struggled to compose a concise command sentence for a task. They often spoke lengthy, unstructured, and descriptive sentences
notes: Smart-speaker context; implies GranPhone voice features need forgiving input (push-to-talk, no wake word, confirmation prompts) or voice as output only.

claim: First impressions of voice interaction among seniors were positive — speech was perceived as simple, efficient, convenient — so voice/TTS is worth offering, but it must tolerate mistakes and teach its own operation; a tutorial is only a stopgap since 'a well-designed user interface must be intuitive enough for novice users without needing any manuals or instruction.'
verbatim_quote: a well-designed user interface must be intuitive enough for novice users without needing any manuals or instruction
notes: Design implications: help users understand how the assistant works, incorporate mistakes/common interaction patterns into design.

claim: Hearing loss is a common barrier to voice/audio interfaces for older adults — TTS output in senior apps should support slow rate, high volume, replay, and always have a visual fallback.
verbatim_quote: hearing loss imposes a significant challenge to the use of voice assistants for many of them
notes: Inference: paper discusses hearing loss re: voice assistants; the TTS-design recommendations are my extrapolation.

claim: Icon style guidance for seniors: use simple, meaningful, and distinctive icons that avoid look-alike neighbors — older adults struggle to distinguish similar-appearing icons and buttons.
verbatim_quote: designers should use simple, meaningful and distinctive icons to promote users' recognition and comprehension of assisted navigation buttons

claim: Icons should be simple and schematic — minimal detail, basic object characteristics — since intricate detail is hard to distinguish at small sizes; apply the 5-second rule (if you can't think of an obvious icon in 5s, no icon will communicate it).
verbatim_quote: Keep the design simple and schematic. Reduce the amount of graphic details by focusing on the basic characteristics of the object rather than creating a highly realistic image in order to speed up recognition. (Intricate details are difficult to distinguish at smaller sizes.)

claim: Smartphone icons in the wild are not designed around seniors' actual needs — a Japanese survey of seniors measured icon intelligibility specifically because older users are 'expected to have the same ability as the youngers' despite mismatched design.
verbatim_quote: older people are usually expected to have the same ability as the youngers to use smartphones with too many applications, which are obviously not based on the practical needs of the senior
notes: English abstract only; full text Japanese. Weak but corroborating.
